summary: A researcher accessed the dark web to collect zero-day vulnerability data, encountering illegal content, hacker tools, and a fund-stealing script.
dilemmas: (i) Ethics of handling illegal data incidentally encountered; (ii) How to store/destroy sensitive research data; (iii) IRB gap for dark-web research; (iv) Obligation to report illegal content to authorities

summary: Three MIT students found vulnerabilities in the MBTA subway ticketing system as a class project and planned to present at DEF CON. The MBTA sued under the CFAA and obtained a gag order; it was later lifted.
dilemmas: (i) Research freedom vs. legal liability; (ii) Using litigation to suppress legitimate security findings; (iii) Free speech rights of security researchers; (iv) Responsible disclosure timeline

summary: Auernheimer scripted enumeration of AT&T's unsecured iPad endpoint, harvesting 114,000 email addresses and ICC-IDs. He shared the data with Gawker. Convicted under CFAA (41 months); vacated on venue grounds.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Is scraping publicly accessible but unintended data unauthorized access under CFAA?; (ii) Responsible disclosure vs. media disclosure to maximize embarrassment; (iii) Chilling effect on legitimate security research; (iv) Corporate negligence vs. researcher culpability

summary: PhD student Soghoian built a web tool generating realistic fake TSA boarding passes to alert Congress to a long-known security flaw. The FBI raided his home; charges were eventually dropped.
dilemmas: (i) Is creating a working exploit to force policy change ethically justified?; (ii) Research freedom vs. real-world risk of tool misuse; (iii) Government pressure to suppress valid security findings; (iv) When does responsible disclosure become irresponsible provocation?

summary: Researchers sent realistic fake phishing emails to university staff and students without consent or prior debriefing to study social engineering responses. Some recipients experienced genuine stress.
dilemmas: (i) Informed consent in deception-based cybersecurity experiments; (ii) Psychological harm to non-consenting participants; (iii) Whether IRBs are equipped to evaluate realistic cyber-deception studies; (iv) Institutional obligations when using own community as test subjects

summary: UMN researchers submitted deliberately buggy/malicious patches to the Linux kernel without consent to test maintainer review processes. Linux banned UMN from future contributions and reverted all prior commits.
dilemmas: (i) Experimenting on open-source community without consent; (ii) Misuse of volunteer maintainer time; (iii) Risk of introducing real vulnerabilities into critical infrastructure; (iv) Publication of methods enabling similar attacks

summary: Researchers studying web censorship placed JavaScript snippets on third-party websites; visiting users' browsers silently participated in the experiment without consent. Users in authoritarian countries faced potential state surveillance.
dilemmas: (i) No informed consent from users whose computers were co-opted; (ii) Placing users at physical/legal risk in authoritarian regimes; (iii) Public interest vs. individual rights; (iv) IRB adequacy for research externalizing risk onto bystanders

summary: CMU researchers discovered a technique to de-anonymize Tor users by running malicious relay nodes. They planned to present at Black Hat but canceled. The FBI allegedly paid ~$1M to use the technique against Silk Road 2.0 users, sweeping thousands of non-criminal Tor users.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Research on human subjects without consent; (ii) Withholding a vulnerability from the affected party (Tor Project); (iii) Financial incentives vs. ethical responsibility; (iv) Using academic research as outsourced law enforcement

summary: Researchers passively captured packets on open public Wi-Fi networks to analyze what personally identifiable information was transmitted in cleartext, finding widespread exposure of emails, login credentials, and location data.
dilemmas: (i) Legality of passive interception of open Wi-Fi traffic (Wiretap Act / ECPA); (ii) Whether 'no login required' implies user consent to interception; (iii) IRB adequacy for research intercepting third-party communications; (iv) Publication alerting both attackers and defenders

summary: Researchers simulated a ransomware attack in a controlled environment to understand propagation patterns. The paper provided sufficiently detailed technical methodology to raise dual-use concerns.
dilemmas: (i) Dual-use publication risk: detailed ransomware implementation as research artifact; (ii) Whether detailed technical methodology should be withheld even when experiment was ethical; (iii) Responsible disclosure to OS/software vendors before publication; (iv) Community norms around weapons-grade research in academic venues

summary: Security researchers at multiple institutions deploy honeypot systems to attract and log real attacker activity without consent. Some cases involve researcher interaction with attackers, raising entrapment concerns.
dilemmas: (i) Is studying criminal activity without consent ethical when 'subjects' are themselves acting illegally?; (ii) Entrapment vs. observation; (iii) Publishing attacker IP addresses and tools; (iv) Liability if honeypot is misused as a lateral pivot by attackers

summary: Birmingham researchers studied keylogging malware behavior in a controlled lab, producing detailed technical documentation of how to implement effective keyloggers and evade detection — with obvious dual-use potential.
dilemmas: (i) Dual-use documentation: keylogger implementation guides as academic research; (ii) Unregulated OS/sensor access as research methodology; (iii) Deception inherent in research design; (iv) Whether publication of offensive tool techniques requires prior vendor notification

summary: A Michigan security team authorized by DC election officials hacked a Washington DC internet voting pilot within 36 hours, gaining full control and modifying vote totals. DC cancelled the system; the team published full technical details.
dilemmas: (i) Does authorized pentesting of election infrastructure risk undermining public trust in democracy?; (ii) Full technical disclosure vs. limiting details that could enable copycat attacks; (iii) Academic freedom to publish results of authorized civic hacking; (iv) Coordination challenges between researchers, vendors, and election officials

institution: MedSec Holdings / Muddy Waters (St. Jude Medical)
summary: MedSec found serious vulnerabilities in St. Jude Medical cardiac implant devices. Rather than disclosing to the vendor, they partnered with investment firm Muddy Waters to short St. Jude's stock and released partial vulnerability details publicly.
dilemmas: (i) Financial conflict of interest in vulnerability disclosure; (ii) Potential patient risk from partial/premature disclosure; (iii) Bypassing coordinated disclosure entirely for profit; (iv) Whether short-selling on security research is legal/ethical

institution: David Levin / Vanguard Cybersecurity / Florida Elections
summary: Pen-tester David Levin tested SQL injection vulnerabilities on a Florida county elections website without written authorization and was arrested for unauthorized access.
dilemmas: (i) Unauthorized testing of public election infrastructure — crime or civic duty?; (ii) Whether pentesting without explicit written authorization can ever be 'ethical'; (iii) Chilling effect on election security research; (iv) Distinction between proof-of-concept testing and malicious intrusion

summary: Harvard researchers reverse-engineered popular mobile applications to expose privacy risks and data leaks, violating app store terms of service and potentially IP rights in the process.
dilemmas: (i) Is reverse engineering software to expose privacy violations legally and ethically permissible?; (ii) Violation of ToS and IP rights in public-interest research; (iii) Responsible disclosure when app developers deny wrongdoing; (iv) IRB adequacy for research involving third-party software artifacts

institution: University of Hawaii & Notre Dame (AI/ML Hijacking)
summary: Researchers identified a supply-chain vulnerability in AI/ML model hosting platforms. After vendors were non-responsive, researchers published publicly to pressure remediation.
dilemmas: (i) How long must researchers wait before publishing when vendors are non-responsive?; (ii) Does 'publish or die' academic incentive conflict with responsible disclosure timelines?; (iii) Liability if publishing before patch leads to exploitation; (iv) Whether AI/ML supply-chain vulnerabilities require a different disclosure framework

summary: NSO Group sold Pegasus zero-click exploit suite to governments worldwide. A 2021 investigation found 50,000+ surveillance targets including journalists, human rights defenders, and opposition leaders across 45+ countries.
dilemmas: (i) Ethics of selling powerful offensive cyber tools to authoritarian governments; (ii) Dual-use technology: legitimate law enforcement vs. repression of civil society; (iii) Liability of tool creators for end-user misuse; (iv) Whether private companies should be permitted to develop nation-state-grade offensive spyware

summary: Three former NSA analysts working for UAE intelligence firm DarkMatter developed iOS zero-click exploits used to surveil dissidents, journalists, and US citizens. DOJ charged them in 2021; they escaped prison via a deferred prosecution agreement and $1.7M fine.
dilemmas: (i) Cyber-mercenaries using US intelligence training to oppress foreign dissidents; (ii) Export control violations (ITAR) for offensive cyber tools; (iii) Accountability gap: deferred prosecution lets former intelligence officers pay their way out; (iv) Revolving door between intelligence agencies and private offensive-cyber firms

institution: Hacking Team Data Breach / Leak Ethics
summary: Italian surveillance company Hacking Team was hacked; 400GB of data leaked to WikiLeaks revealing sales to Sudan, Ethiopia, and Bahrain. Researchers and journalists mined the data to expose clients and zero-days.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Research ethics of using stolen/leaked corporate data; (ii) Whether exposing surveillance vendors justifies privacy violations of their employees; (iii) Researchers re-releasing zero-day exploits found in leaked data; (iv) Corporate accountability for selling offensive tools to authoritarian states

institution: J. Alex Halderman / Georgia Dominion Voting Machines
summary: University of Michigan professor Halderman was given court-supervised access to Georgia's Dominion voting machines and developed proof-of-concept attacks. His sealed report was later partially unsealed and seized upon by election-denial conspiracy theorists.
dilemmas: (i) Academic freedom vs. potential to fuel election misinformation; (ii) Whether sealed vulnerability research can remain secret in an adversarial legal setting; (iii) Risk that legitimate security findings are weaponized for political disinformation; (iv) Tension between public right to know and protecting public trust in elections

summary: Citizen Lab (University of Toronto) repeatedly identified and exposed governments using FinFisher spyware to surveil dissidents and journalists in Bahrain, Ethiopia, and Turkey, potentially tipping off targeted governments to improve their tradecraft.
dilemmas: (i) Does publishing detailed attribution of surveillance operations tip off abusive governments?; (ii) Researcher responsibility to notify both victims and software vendors; (iii) Balance between academic publication norms and protecting at-risk human rights defenders; (iv) Whether Western companies should face consequences for selling spyware to authoritarian buyers

institution: Justin Shafer / Patterson Dental / FBI Raids
summary: Texas dental IT researcher Shafer found patient health data on a publicly accessible anonymous FTP server and reported it responsibly. Patterson Dental complained to the FBI; Shafer's home was raided three times. He spent 8 months in pretrial detention on cyberstalking charges (for Facebook posts), ultimately pleading to one misdemeanor.
dilemmas: (i) 'Shoot the messenger' — vendor weaponizing CFAA against the person who exposed their negligence; (ii) Using cyberstalking statutes to silence researcher criticism of government overreach; (iii) Chilling effect: other researchers stopped disclosing after the raids; (iv) Pretrial detention as punishment before conviction

summary: Swartz bulk-downloaded ~4.8M academic articles from JSTOR using MIT's network, apparently intending to release them freely. JSTOR settled civilly and dropped charges; federal prosecutors charged him with 13 CFAA felonies (up to 50 years). Swartz died by suicide two days after rejecting a plea deal.
outcome: Charged (case ended with death of defendant)
dilemmas: (i) CFAA overcriminalization — was exceeding ToS really a felony?; (ii) Prosecutorial overreach when the victim (JSTOR) dropped the case; (iii) Open-access ideology vs. intellectual property law; (iv) Criminal penalties disproportionate to actual harm

summary: Hutchins stopped the WannaCry ransomware by registering its kill-switch domain. Months later the FBI arrested him at DEF CON, alleging he helped develop the Kronos banking trojan in 2014–2015. He pleaded guilty to two CFAA counts and was sentenced to time served.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Should past black-hat activity negate subsequent white-hat contributions?; (ii) Arresting a researcher at a security conference as a deterrent tactic; (iii) Fairness of prosecuting juvenile/early-career offenses years later; (iv) Community trust in law enforcement collaboration with researchers

summary: QOMPLX relaunched PunkSpider at DEF CON — a tool that mass-crawls the web for SQL injection, XSS, and path-traversal vulnerabilities and publishes results in a searchable public database, exposing real flaws in Kickstarter and LendingTree before notification.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Public disclosure of vulnerabilities before vendor notification; (ii) Dual-use: security tool vs. attack enablement; (iii) Scanning sites without owner consent (potential CFAA exposure); (iv) Whether 'pressure through shame' is an ethical remediation strategy

institution: University of Michigan / FTP: The Forgotten Cloud
summary: Michigan researchers scanned the entire IPv4 address space without permission to identify anonymous FTP servers leaking sensitive data, finding over 1 million open servers. The FBI used the data but so did ransomware actors (TheDarkOverlord).
dilemmas: (i) Ethical permissibility of internet-wide scanning without operator consent; (ii) Legal exposure under CFAA for automated access to systems not owned by researchers; (iii) Responsible disclosure when 1M+ vulnerable systems cannot all be notified; (iv) Dual-use: FBI used findings, but so did ransomware actors

institution: Indiana University / Xiao Wang FBI Investigation
summary: Prominent cybersecurity/privacy professor Xiao Wang had his home raided by the FBI in spring 2025 amid questions about undisclosed Chinese research funding from 2017–2018. No arrests or criminal charges had been filed at time of the raid.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
outcome: Under investigation (no charges filed at time of reporting)
dilemmas: (i) Duty to disclose foreign research funding on US federal grant applications; (ii) Academic freedom vs. national security concerns about foreign research entanglement; (iii) Due process when law enforcement raids without public criminal charges; (iv) Chilling effect on international research collaboration

institution: Ola Bini / Ecuador / Privacy Tool Developer
summary: Swedish open-source developer and privacy-tool contributor Ola Bini was arrested in Ecuador concurrent with Assange's UK arrest. Prosecutors cited possession of technical books and Japanese anime as evidence of hacking intent. He was held without charges for months.
dilemmas: (i) Criminalization of possession of security tools and technical literature as evidence of malicious intent; (ii) Politically motivated prosecution of security researchers; (iii) Due process rights of open-source developers; (iv) Chilling effect on privacy-tool development

institution: Crisis Text Line / Data Sharing with Loris.ai
summary: Crisis Text Line, a mental-health crisis nonprofit, shared detailed conversation data with Loris.ai, a for-profit spinoff, to train AI models sold to corporations. The arrangement was buried in the privacy policy; public outrage and investigations followed.
dilemmas: (i) Informed consent: crisis users cannot meaningfully consent to commercial AI training of their data; (ii) Re-identification risk from 'anonymized' highly sensitive mental health data; (iii) Conflict of interest when nonprofit mission is compromised by commercial data partnerships; (iv) Whether 'disclosed in privacy policy' constitutes adequate consent

institution: Kennesaw State University / Georgia Election Server
summary: Logan Lamb found Georgia's entire election infrastructure server publicly accessible at KSU, containing voter registration data, passwords, and election management files. KSU wiped the server before the FBI could examine it during the subsequent investigation.
outcome: No charges filed (KSU; evidence destruction concerns)
dilemmas: (i) Responsible disclosure failure when institutions do not respond to researcher notifications; (ii) Destruction of evidence after a researcher goes public; (iii) Whether researchers have an obligation to escalate beyond the institution when critical infrastructure is at risk; (iv) Accountability gap when election infrastructure is housed at an academic institution

institution: Jason Parker / Georgia Voter Cancellation Portal
summary: Independent researcher Jason Parker found a critical flaw in Georgia's online voter-cancellation portal: anyone knowing a voter's name, birth date, and county could cancel any voter's registration. He notified the Secretary of State's office; the office denied receiving the notification. ProPublica published the story; the flaw was quickly patched.
dilemmas: (i) When a government office denies receiving researcher notification, what recourse does the researcher have?; (ii) Timing of media disclosure for critical election infrastructure vulnerabilities; (iii) Risk that responsible disclosure of election bugs becomes fodder for disinformation; (iv) Whether election officials' denial of researcher contact constitutes bad faith

summary: The FBI operated a seized dark-web child exploitation site (Playpen) for 13 days, deploying a malware exploit (NIT) to de-anonymize ~1,500 Tor user suspects globally. A single warrant authorized the operation across 120+ countries. DOJ dropped some cases rather than reveal NIT technical details.
outcome: Courts split on admissibility; some cases dropped
dilemmas: (i) Government use of malware as investigative technique without targeted warrants; (ii) Single warrant authorizing hacking of computers across 120+ countries; (iii) DOJ choosing to drop prosecutions rather than disclose offensive tools; (iv) Does fighting CSAM justify warrantless global hacking of Tor users?

summary: IOActive researchers found critical flaws in smart city infrastructure — traffic sensors, emergency-alert systems, water-control systems — through some unauthorized testing ('fire and forget' scan-and-test). Vendors were slow to patch; IOActive published technical details at DEF CON.
dilemmas: (i) Scanning municipal critical infrastructure without written permission; (ii) Full technical disclosure of infrastructure vulnerabilities when patches remain unavailable; (iii) Risk that published details of water/traffic attacks could cause physical harm; (iv) Whether researchers must wait longer when targets are critical infrastructure

summary: iSight Partners discovered Russian group Sandworm exploiting a Windows zero-day (CVE-2014-4114) to target NATO and Ukrainian government systems. iSight had used the intelligence for weeks before coordinating a patch release with Microsoft, monetizing it as a client intelligence product.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Private threat-intelligence firms monetizing zero-day knowledge vs. immediate public disclosure; (ii) Whether commercial security sector should have a legal disclosure obligation; (iii) Conflict between client confidentiality and warning undefended third parties; (iv) Government contractors holding offensive capabilities creates asymmetric vulnerability landscape

summary: Setting up a honeynet at University of Dhaka attracted over 63,000 attacks in 12 days, providing data on real attacker behavior and tactics.
dilemmas: (i) Ethical interaction with cybercriminals without encouraging illegal behavior; (ii) Entrapment vs. observation; (iii) Non-consent experimentation on criminals

summary: JHU researchers deployed high-interaction honeypots to study real attacker behavior and TTPs in depth.
dilemmas: (i) Ethical interaction with cybercriminals without encouraging illegal behavior; (ii) Entrapment vs. observation; (iii) Non-consent experimentation on criminals

summary: McDanel, a former employee, emailed ~5,600 customers warning that the company's webmail system displayed login credentials in the browser address bar in plaintext. He was convicted under the CFAA and sentenced to 16 months. Conviction was later overturned after prosecutors admitted error.
dilemmas: (i) Should warning customers about a security flaw ever count as a 'malicious code' offense?; (ii) What recourse exists for a wrongful felony conviction already served?; (iii) Chilling effect of CFAA's vague 'damage' language on good-faith disclosure

summary: After donating to a tsunami relief site and receiving no confirmation page, security consultant Daniel Cuthbert manually tested the donation page for phishing signs. He was convicted under the UK Computer Misuse Act and fined — the first such conviction under that section.
dilemmas: (i) Does intent matter under strict-liability computer-misuse statutes?; (ii) Should consumer self-protection checks ever be criminalized?; (iii) Career destruction disproportionate to harm caused

institution: Josh Renaud / Missouri DESE (St. Louis Post-Dispatch)
summary: Reporter Josh Renaud found teacher Social Security numbers exposed in a state website's HTML source code, verified it responsibly, and waited for a fix before publishing. Missouri Governor Parson publicly called him a 'hacker' and referred the case to prosecutors. No criminal intent was found; case was closed without charges.
dilemmas: (i) Should governments be able to relabel 'view source' inspection as criminal hacking to deflect blame?; (ii) Press freedom vs. official retaliation for embarrassing disclosures; (iii) Use of vague hacking rhetoric to chill future security journalism

summary: Finisterre found DJI's wildcard SSL certificate and AWS keys exposed on GitHub, accessing customer flight logs, passports, and IDs. After reporting through DJI's bug bounty, DJI allegedly threatened CFAA charges and required a restrictive NDA before paying the $30,000 bounty. Finisterre declined and published the dispute publicly.
dilemmas: (i) Can bug bounty confidentiality terms be used to suppress legitimate findings?; (ii) Threatening prosecution against a researcher acting within a company's disclosed scope; (iii) Power imbalance between corporate legal teams and individual researchers

institution: Joseph Sullivan / Uber Data Breach Cover-Up
summary: Ten days after testifying to the FTC about Uber's security, Sullivan learned of a breach of 57M records. He arranged a $100K payment to hackers framed as a bug bounty and concealed the breach from the FTC. Convicted of obstruction and misprision of a felony; sentenced to three years' probation and $50K fine.
dilemmas: (i) Personal criminal liability of security executives for breach cover-ups; (ii) Where is the line between 'incident response' and witness tampering/concealment?; (iii) Should corporate leadership above the CSO share equal culpability?

institution: Flavio Garcia / University of Birmingham (VW & Thales)
summary: Garcia and Dutch colleagues cracked the Megamos Crypto algorithm used in vehicle immobilizers across 26 car brands. Volkswagen and Thales obtained a UK High Court injunction blocking publication for ~2 years; it was lifted after researchers agreed to redact a single sentence.
dilemmas: (i) Should a manufacturer be able to suppress academic publication of a flaw in its own product?; (ii) Reverse engineering legitimately purchased hardware vs. 'breach of confidence'; (iii) Public's right to know about car-theft vulnerabilities vs. risk of enabling theft

institution: Radboud University / Bart Jacobs (NXP / Mifare Classic)
summary: After privately notifying NXP and the Dutch government, Radboud researchers prepared to publish a paper breaking the Mifare Classic transit-card chip (used by London's Oyster card). NXP sued; a Dutch court rejected the injunction, ruling academic freedom outweighed NXP's commercial interest.
dilemmas: (i) Should commercial harm from a disclosed flaw ever justify suppressing peer-reviewed research?; (ii) Academic freedom vs. critical-infrastructure (transit) security concerns; (iii) Adequacy of advance confidential notification before publication

institution: Eric McCarty / University of Southern California
summary: McCarty exploited a SQL injection flaw in USC's online applicant database, downloading seven records from a database containing 275,000+ applicants' SSNs, before anonymously reporting it. He pleaded guilty to CFAA charges; sentenced to probation and $36,800 restitution.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Does proving a vulnerability by exploiting it cross from research into a prosecutable crime?; (ii) Proportionality of felony record/restitution vs. alerting the university; (iii) Effect of 'bragging' online on prosecutorial framing of intent

summary: Lynn resigned from ISS on the morning of his Black Hat talk to warn that Cisco routers could be exploited for a self-propagating 'router worm.' Cisco and ISS obtained a federal injunction barring further dissemination; Lynn agreed to a permanent injunction surrendering all related materials.
dilemmas: (i) Using copyright/trade-secret claims to suppress a security warning after the fact; (ii) Researcher's duty to disclose imminent internet-scale risk vs. employer's IP claims; (iii) Chilling effect of corporate legal muscle on conference speakers

summary: A 16-year-old found SQL injection and access-control flaws exposing ~5 million student records. After Blackboard ignored him for months and Follett never responded, he pushed a mass notification to students, parents, and staff. Blackboard required an NDA before further conversation; the school suspended him for two days.
dilemmas: (i) Is escalating to a mass alert ethical when normal disclosure channels are ignored by vendors?; (ii) Vendors using NDAs to control a minor researcher's ability to discuss findings; (iii) Industry-wide underinvestment in security for children's data

summary: A former AWS engineer exploited misconfigured cloud storage to access data on ~106 million Capital One customers and planted cryptomining software on compromised servers. Convicted of wire fraud and computer intrusion; resentenced to time served, five years supervised release, and $40.7M restitution.
dilemmas: (i) Where is the line between legitimate cloud-misconfiguration research and felony data theft?; (ii) Should mental health and personal circumstances factor into sentencing for large-scale breaches?; (iii) Appellate oversight of 'too lenient' sentences for first-time offenders

summary: Volunteer research group Sakura Samurai targeted organizations with published VDPs, finding exposed credentials giving access to 100,000+ UN employee records and credentials across 26 Indian government departments. They limited actions to verification and disclosed through official channels; no charges were filed.
dilemmas: (i) Does scanning specifically because an org has a VDP make later 'out of scope' findings authorized?; (ii) Should past black-hat convictions disqualify someone from later legitimate research?; (iii) Reliance on government agencies to respond competently once notified

summary: Puffer demonstrated to a county official and a reporter that the district clerk's new wireless network had no security. He was indicted on two CFAA-related counts carrying up to five years each; a jury acquitted him in about 15 minutes.
dilemmas: (i) Should demonstrating a flaw to officials and media be treated identically to malicious intrusion?; (ii) Use of prosecution to deflect blame from the agency's own security failure; (iii) Jury nullification as a check on overbroad computer-crime statutes

institution: Clayton Taylor Dillard / Wake Internal Medicine (Wi-Fi)
summary: An IT consultant accessed an unsecured medical practice wireless network, obtained patient billing and insurance records, and contacted the press and patients directly to publicize the clinic's lax security. He pleaded guilty to wireless computer intrusion — the first such conviction in the US.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Why did near-identical facts (Puffer acquitted, Dillard convicted) produce opposite outcomes?; (ii) Contacting patients/press directly vs. notifying the practice first; (iii) Patient privacy harm from the disclosure method itself, separate from the underlying flaw

institution: Charlie Miller & Chris Valasek / Jeep Cherokee
summary: Researchers remotely disabled a Jeep's transmission and brakes over its cellular-connected infotainment system while a journalist drove on the highway. This forced a recall of ~1.4 million vehicles; owners filed a class-action suit against FCA alleging the company knew of the architectural flaw since 2011.
outcome: No charges filed; civil suit allowed to proceed
dilemmas: (i) Is a dramatic public stunt the only way to force a slow-moving manufacturer to patch a safety-critical flaw?; (ii) Consumer standing to sue over a vulnerability patched before real-world exploitation; (iii) Coupling safety-critical vehicle systems to internet-facing infotainment

institution: David Ross ('Connor Goodwolf') / City of Columbus Ransomware
summary: After Columbus downplayed a Rhysida ransomware breach, independent researcher Ross shared proof with local media that police personnel files, undercover officer identities, and 400,000+ residents' data were exposed. Columbus sued him and obtained a TRO; the city dropped the suit ~two months later under pressure from the EFF.
dilemmas: (i) Suing a whistleblower to manage a government's own breach-disclosure narrative; (ii) First Amendment limits on restraining someone from discussing already-public leaked data; (iii) Power asymmetry between a city government and an individual researcher

summary: When Newag-built Impuls trains began locking up after independent-shop maintenance, Dragon Sector reverse-engineered the onboard software and found GPS-triggered lockout code designed to disable trains serviced by competitors. Newag sued for copyright infringement and defamation; at the first hearing Newag conceded researchers had not modified any train software.
dilemmas: (i) Manufacturers using anti-repair 'DRM' embedded in safety-critical infrastructure; (ii) Suing researchers for exposing the lockout rather than addressing it (right-to-repair); (iii) Criminal investigations opened against disclosers rather than the manufacturer

institution: Wesley Wineberg / Facebook / Instagram Bug Bounty
summary: Through Facebook's bug bounty, Wineberg found an RCE flaw on an Instagram server, then continued probing and obtained SSL/signing keys and access to Amazon storage buckets. Facebook's CSO contacted Wineberg's employer to push back; Facebook denied threatening legal action but said further exfiltration was unauthorized.
dilemmas: (i) Where does legitimate 'proof of impact' end and unauthorized data exfiltration begin within a bug bounty's scope?; (ii) Going around a researcher to pressure their employer instead of addressing the researcher directly; (iii) Ambiguity in bug bounty terms about how far a researcher may go to demonstrate severity

summary: While fixing a client's software, an IT contractor found a hardcoded plaintext database password in an executable, used it to confirm the scope of exposure (nearly 700,000 customer records), and reported it. Modern Solution reported him to police instead. He was ultimately convicted of unlawful data access and fined €3,000.
dilemmas: (i) Should using a password the vendor itself left in plaintext constitute criminal 'unauthorized access'?; (ii) Criminalizing the verification step required to confirm a vulnerability is real; (iii) Disparity between vendor's negligence (unpunished) and researcher's penalty (criminal record)

summary: Former Intel contractor Schwartz ran a password-cracking tool against Intel's systems, saying he wanted to demonstrate that security had deteriorated since his departure. Convicted of three Oregon felony counts; sentenced to probation, 480 hours community service, and $68,000 restitution. Conviction set aside and expunged in 2007.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) Should 'improving security' justify unauthorized access against a former employer's systems?; (ii) Multi-decade reputational and financial cost of a later-overturned felony conviction; (iii) Employer's choice to pursue criminal prosecution rather than civil/internal remedies

summary: Russian ElcomSoft employee Sklyarov was arrested by the FBI immediately after his DEF CON talk on breaking Adobe eBook encryption — the first criminal charge under the DMCA. Held in custody then under travel restriction before a deal requiring his testimony against ElcomSoft in exchange for dropped charges.
outcome: Charged (charges dropped in exchange for testimony)
dilemmas: (i) Should conduct legal in a researcher's home country (Russia) trigger US criminal arrest at a US conference?; (ii) Conference attendance as a venue for law enforcement action against speakers; (iii) Using one defendant's testimony as leverage to convict their employer

institution: Matthew Green & bunnie Huang v. DOJ (DMCA / Section 1201)
summary: Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green and engineer Andrew 'bunnie' Huang filed a First Amendment challenge (via EFF) against Section 1201 of the DMCA, arguing it unconstitutionally prevented Green from publishing security research on commercial devices and Huang from building a legitimate video-stream device. Green said DMCA fear caused him to decline to investigate certain devices and chilled him from disclosing vulnerabilities. The DC Circuit ultimately upheld the DMCA's anti-circumvention provisions in 2024, finding they regulate conduct not speech.
dilemmas: (i) Does the DMCA's anti-circumvention provision unconstitutionally chill security research that requires bypassing DRM?; (ii) Should researchers be required to apply for triennial exemptions to do work that would otherwise be protected fair use?; (iii) How does the chilling effect of potential prosecution shape what security vulnerabilities get investigated and disclosed?; (iv) When researchers self-censor to avoid legal risk, who bears the cost in terms of undetected vulnerabilities?

institution: In Re Yahoo! Inc. Customer Data Security Breach Litigation
summary: Yahoo suffered a series of massive data breaches (2013–2016) affecting all 3 billion user accounts. Yahoo's security team was aware of the 2014 breach for over two years before public disclosure; executives disclosed the breaches only when required during Verizon's acquisition negotiations. Shareholders and users filed securities class action suits alleging Yahoo's leadership concealed material information about the breaches from investors and the public.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) At what point does delayed breach disclosure cross from incident response into material omission for securities fraud?; (ii) What is a CSO/CISO's personal duty when corporate leadership decides to delay disclosure?; (iii) Acquisition context: does a pending merger change the calculus of when a breach must be disclosed?; (iv) Are current securities laws adequate to deter corporate concealment of large-scale breaches?

institution: In Re Okta, Inc. Securities Litigation
summary: Okta suffered a breach by the Lapsus$ hacking group in January 2022 but did not publicly disclose it for over two months, and only after a hacker posted screenshots publicly. When Okta did disclose, executives initially downplayed the scope, later admitting that all Okta customer support users' data had been accessed. Shareholders filed a securities class action alleging Okta made materially false and misleading statements about the breach's scope and timing.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) When a company minimizes a breach publicly while knowing the full scope internally, is that fraud or legitimate incident response?; (ii) What is the appropriate disclosure timeline when breach scope is still being investigated?; (iii) Does downplaying a breach to avoid stock impact constitute securities fraud even if the company later corrects the record?; (iv) How should security executives balance legal counsel's advice against ethical obligations to customers?

institution: In Re Equifax Inc. Securities Litigation
summary: Equifax suffered a breach in May 2017 exposing the personal data of 147 million Americans. Equifax's CISO and CIO sold millions in company stock weeks after the breach was discovered internally but before public disclosure. The SEC investigated for insider trading; the CISO was later indicted on insider trading charges. Shareholders filed a massive securities class action; Equifax ultimately settled with the FTC, CFPB, and states for $575M+.
dilemmas: (i) Does selling stock after learning of a breach but before public disclosure constitute insider trading, regardless of intent?; (ii) What personal criminal liability do security executives bear for their company's breach concealment?; (iii) Should a CISO who discovers a breach be required to immediately notify the board even if doing so triggers premature disclosure?; (iv) Are mandatory breach disclosure timelines the right policy lever, or do they just create liability without improving security?

institution: AFGE v. OPM (Federal Employee / Security Clearance Data Breach)
summary: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) suffered a breach in 2014–2015 that exposed background investigation files of 21.5 million current and former federal employees, including SF-86 security clearance forms with deeply sensitive personal information. OPM had been warned repeatedly about its poor cybersecurity posture but failed to act. The American Federation of Government Employees sued; courts ultimately dismissed on standing grounds, but the case raised profound questions about government accountability for protecting its employees' most sensitive data.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) What duty of care does a government agency owe its employees when it holds their most sensitive personal and national security data?; (ii) When repeated security warnings are ignored and a catastrophic breach occurs, who bears personal accountability?; (iii) Should federal employees whose security clearance files were stolen have a right to sue for damages?; (iv) Does sovereign immunity effectively shield government agencies from accountability for catastrophic security failures?

summary: hiQ, a data analytics company, scraped public LinkedIn profiles using automated bots to build workforce analytics products. LinkedIn sent a cease-and-desist and blocked hiQ's access. hiQ sued; the Ninth Circuit twice ruled that scraping publicly accessible data likely does not violate the CFAA because 'without authorization' requires a gate/barrier the scraper bypassed. The Supreme Court vacated and remanded in light of Van Buren. Ultimately hiQ settled, agreeing to a $500K judgment and permanent injunction after LinkedIn won on breach-of-contract grounds using fake profile creation.
dilemmas: (i) Is scraping publicly accessible data 'unauthorized access' under the CFAA if no password or authentication barrier was bypassed?; (ii) Can a company weaponize the CFAA to prevent a competitor from accessing data that users themselves made public?; (iii) Where is the line between lawful data collection for research/analysis and commercial exploitation of user-generated public data?; (iv) Does the CFAA's broad interpretation give large platforms de facto monopoly control over public data?

institution: Universal City Studios v. Corley / Reimerdes (DeCSS / DMCA)
summary: 2600 Magazine publisher Eric Corley (Emmanuel Goldstein) posted the DeCSS code — a program that decrypted DVD copy protection — on his website and linked to other sites hosting it. The movie studios sued under the DMCA's anti-trafficking provision. The Second Circuit upheld the injunction, ruling that computer code posting is regulable conduct under intermediate First Amendment scrutiny and that the DMCA's anti-trafficking provision was constitutional. The case became the defining early test of whether publishing security-relevant code is protected speech.
dilemmas: (i) Is publishing functional security/encryption code protected First Amendment speech?; (ii) Can the DMCA's anti-trafficking provision constitutionally prohibit publication of code that has legitimate research and interoperability uses?; (iii) Does linking to a site hosting prohibited code make a publisher liable under the DMCA?; (iv) Who gets to define the boundary between security research tools and circumvention devices?

institution: DVD Copy Control Assn v. Bunner (DeCSS — California)
summary: In a parallel California state court case to Corley, the DVD Copy Control Association sued Andrew Bunner for posting DeCSS under trade secret law (not DMCA). The California Court of Appeal initially upheld a preliminary injunction as a prior restraint on speech, but the California Supreme Court reversed — ruling that the First Amendment required a fuller inquiry before restraining publication, since the code had already spread widely across the internet. The case raised the question of whether trade secret law could suppress already-public security information.
dilemmas: (i) Can trade secret law justify a prior restraint on publication of security-relevant code that has already spread widely on the internet?; (ii) At what point does information become 'too public' to still qualify as a protectable trade secret?; (iii) Does the First Amendment protect redistribution of security code even if the original acquisition was improper?; (iv) Should courts balance the chilling effect on security research before granting injunctions against code publication?

institution: Davidson & Associates v. Jung (Battle.net / bnetd reverse engineering)
summary: Developers reverse-engineered Blizzard's Battle.net gaming service to build 'bnetd,' a free open-source server that let players run their own game servers. Blizzard sued under the DMCA and breach of the end-user license agreement (EULA). The Eighth Circuit ruled against the developers, finding that the EULA's prohibition on reverse engineering was enforceable and that reverse engineering to achieve interoperability did not qualify for the DMCA's interoperability exception because the developers had agreed to the EULA. The case chilled open-source interoperability work.
dilemmas: (i) Can an EULA contractually waive the DMCA's statutory right to reverse engineer for interoperability?; (ii) Is building a compatible open-source alternative to a proprietary service a legitimate security/research activity or IP infringement?; (iii) Should agreeing to a ToS/EULA strip a researcher of rights they would otherwise have under the DMCA's interoperability exception?; (iv) How does this ruling affect security researchers who need to reverse-engineer software they've licensed to find vulnerabilities?

institution: Bernstein v. US Dept. of State (Snuffle encryption export case)
summary: UC Berkeley grad student Daniel Bernstein wrote an encryption program called 'Snuffle' and wanted to publish it and an academic paper explaining it. The State Department classified the software as a 'munition' under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), requiring an export license to publish. EFF represented Bernstein; the Ninth Circuit ultimately ruled that source code is speech protected by the First Amendment and that the ITAR licensing scheme was an unconstitutional prior restraint. The case was foundational in establishing that encryption source code is protected expression and helped end ITAR controls on encryption.
dilemmas: (i) Is encryption source code 'speech' protected by the First Amendment, or purely functional 'conduct' that can be regulated without First Amendment scrutiny?; (ii) Can the government require a license before a researcher publishes an academic paper containing functional encryption code?; (iii) Do national security interests in controlling encryption export justify prior restraint on academic publication?; (iv) How should the law treat dual-use academic research that has both civilian security value and potential military/intelligence applications?

institution: Cobell v. Norton — BIA Internet Disconnection / Security Audit
summary: In a class action over mismanagement of Native American trust accounts, a court-appointed security expert found that the Bureau of Indian Affairs' computer systems were so insecure that the judge ordered the entire Interior Department's internet connectivity disconnected until security could be verified. The case raised profound questions about what a court can order when government IT security failures endanger beneficiaries' financial data — and who bears accountability when critical government systems fail basic security standards.
dilemmas: (i) Can a court order a government agency to disconnect from the internet as a security remedy?; (ii) What accountability mechanisms exist when a government agency's repeated security failures endanger the financial data of a vulnerable population?; (iii) Who should conduct security audits of government systems — internal auditors, independent experts, or adversarial testers?; (iv) When a security audit reveals catastrophic failure, how should findings be disclosed without creating additional risk?

institution: United States v. Verkada Inc. (Mass Surveillance Camera Breach)
summary: Hacker collective Tillie Kottmann breached Verkada, a cloud-based security camera company, accessing live feeds from 150,000+ cameras inside hospitals, prisons, Tesla factories, and schools. Kottmann claimed the breach was meant to expose the pervasiveness of mass surveillance. Verkada was later fined $2.95M by the FTC for inadequate security practices. Kottmann was indicted on conspiracy charges; the case raised questions about whether exposing surveillance infrastructure is a legitimate form of security activism.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
outcome: Indicted (Kottmann); FTC civil action against Verkada ($2.95M fine)
dilemmas: (i) Is breaching a surveillance company to expose its reach a form of protected political/security activism or straightforward criminal hacking?; (ii) Does the target being a surveillance company change the ethical calculus of an unauthorized breach?; (iii) What accountability should cloud security camera vendors face when their poor security exposes sensitive environments like hospitals and prisons?; (iv) When a vendor's negligence enables mass surveillance exposure, who bears moral responsibility — the hacker or the vendor?

institution: BlackSuit Ransomware / KCKPD / Wired & KCUR (Kansas City Police Misconduct List)
summary: The BlackSuit ransomware gang breached the Kansas City, Kansas Police Department in May 2024, stealing over 1TB of data including a secret Giglio/Veracity Disclosure List naming 62 current and former officers with misconduct so serious it could impeach their testimony. After KCKPD refused to pay the ransom, BlackSuit published the data. Transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets hosted the data, restricting access to journalists, researchers, and defense attorneys. WIRED and KCUR published an investigation revealing officers with serious misconduct records — including sexual harassment, excessive force, and false arrests — who had been retained or promoted.
dilemmas: (i) Is it ethical for journalists and researchers to analyze and publish findings from data stolen by ransomware criminals, when the findings expose genuine government misconduct?; (ii) Does restricting access to journalists, researchers, and defense attorneys adequately mitigate the harms of publishing stolen government data?; (iii) Does the public interest in police accountability ever justify using data obtained by criminal actors?; (iv) What is the difference between this and the Hacking Team case — does the target's identity (law enforcement vs. surveillance vendor) change the ethical analysis?

institution: IT Consultant Fined for Exposing Shoddy Security (Germany / Modern Solution parallel)
summary: A German IT consultant discovered a security vulnerability at a client's system and reported it. Instead of addressing the flaw, the company reported the consultant to police. The consultant was fined for unauthorized access under German law, even though their intent was to expose and report the vulnerability. The case closely parallels the Modern Solution GmbH case (C056) and reflects a broader pattern in German jurisprudence of criminalizing good-faith vulnerability verification.
dilemmas: (i) Should accessing a system to verify the scope of a vulnerability you discovered constitute criminal 'unauthorized access'?; (ii) Is reporting a security flaw to the company that hired you sufficient authorization to investigate it?; (iii) How does German computer crime law compare to the CFAA in its treatment of good-faith security researchers?; (iv) What legal safe harbors should exist for contractors who discover vulnerabilities in systems they are hired to work on?

institution: Microsoft / Nightmare Eclipse (Windows Defender & BitLocker Zero-Days)
summary: An anonymous researcher known as 'Nightmare Eclipse' publicly disclosed six unpatched Windows vulnerabilities — including flaws in Defender and BitLocker — after alleging that Microsoft deleted their MSRC (Security Response Center) account, withheld bounty payments, and removed their attribution from an advisory. Three of the six disclosed vulnerabilities (BlueHammer, RedSun, UnDefend) were subsequently exploited in real-world attacks and added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit publicly threatened criminal prosecution; the researcher was also banned from GitHub and GitLab. The cybersecurity community largely sided with the researcher, with veterans warning Microsoft's stance would chill future disclosure.
intent: Ambiguous / gray area (mixed or unclear intent)
dilemmas: (i) When a company allegedly mistreats a researcher — deleting their account, withholding bounty payments, removing attribution — does that researcher bear ethical responsibility for subsequently publishing unpatched vulnerabilities?; (ii) Is 'full disclosure' of an unpatched vulnerability ever ethically justified as a last resort against an unresponsive or hostile vendor?; (iii) Does threatening a researcher with criminal prosecution for disclosing bugs create a chilling effect that ultimately harms users more than the disclosure itself?; (iv) Who bears moral responsibility when a researcher-disclosed vulnerability is exploited in the wild — the researcher or the vendor that failed to patch it?

institution: DJI / Researcher Bug Bounty Quarrel (Kevin Finisterre — extended / SecurityWeek)
summary: Security researcher Kevin Finisterre found DJI's wildcard SSL certificate and AWS S3 bucket access keys exposed on GitHub, potentially exposing customer flight logs, passports, and ID documents. When he reported through DJI's newly launched bug bounty program, DJI allegedly threatened CFAA prosecution and demanded he sign a restrictive NDA before receiving the $30,000 bounty. DJI disputed Finisterre's characterization. Finisterre declined the money and published his account publicly. The case became a template for how bug bounty programs can be used to silence researchers rather than reward them.
dilemmas: (i) Can a bug bounty program's NDA terms be used to effectively suppress a researcher's ability to discuss findings that are already known to the company?; (ii) Is threatening CFAA prosecution against a researcher who operated within a company's own published bug bounty scope an abuse of the legal process?; (iii) What power imbalances exist between corporate legal teams and individual researchers, and how should bug bounty programs be regulated to address them?; (iv) Does a vendor's threat of prosecution after the fact constitute retroactive withdrawal of implied authorization to test?

summary: Academic researchers published a holistic study of WinPot ATM jackpotting malware — a strain used by criminal groups to force ATMs to dispense cash — analyzing its attack vectors, exploitation techniques, and defensive countermeasures in detail. The paper provided comprehensive technical documentation of how ATM jackpotting works, raising dual-use concerns that the level of technical detail could serve as an implementation guide for criminal actors even as it aimed to advance defensive knowledge.
dilemmas: (i) How much technical detail is appropriate in academic publications about criminal malware when the same detail that helps defenders also helps attackers?; (ii) Should researchers publishing analyses of criminal tools be required to coordinate with affected vendors (ATM manufacturers, banks) before publication?; (iii) Is studying and publishing criminal malware ethically different from studying and publishing proof-of-concept researcher-written exploits?; (iv) What responsibility do academic publishers and program committees bear for the dual-use risk of papers they accept?
